title: Decisions
bridge: C uses `if (...) { } else if (...) { } else { }`, `&&`, `||`, `!` and `switch`, exactly like C++ and Java. In C, any non-zero number counts as true and 0 is false, so `if (count)` means "if count isn't 0". `bool` (from `<stdbool.h>`) prints as 1 or 0.

exercises.title: Grades
exercises.prompt: Write char grade(int score): 'A' for 80+, 'B' for 65+, 'C' for 50+, otherwise 'F'.

exercises.title: Pump controller
exercises.prompt: Write bool pump_should_run(int moisture, bool pump_on). Turn on below 30. Turn off above 60. Between 30 and 60, keep doing what it's doing (so it doesn't flick on and off).

tests.hint_if_fail: Between 30 and 60, keep the pump as it is: return pump_on.

hints: Three cases: dry, wet, in between.
if (moisture < 30) return true; if (moisture > 60) return false; return pump_on;

quiz.q: In C, is 5 true or false?
Why keep the pump's state between 30 and 60?
choices: So it doesn't rapidly switch on and off around one number
quiz.why: That gap is called hysteresis; real controllers use it.

explain: Explain decisions to someone who has never programmed, in your own words, with an example you make up.
